line: He observes the country closely from the litter; its outline is engraved in his mind (I.8 ¶87). *(Drafted.)*
He wants the principal features named for their country and its great citizens, and the rivers, gulfs and capes by their shape (I.11 ¶63). *(Drafted.)*
He plans to make an explosive substance to spare the powder (II.3 ¶6). *(Drafted.)*
He had made his companions promise not to fire without need, and asks them to avoid any ill-timed shot so as not to signal their presence near the coast (II.3 ¶7; II.4 ¶3). *(Drafted.)*
For the ditch he has nitro-glycerine made anew, since two to three feet of soil lie over granite, and it does its accustomed work (II.7 ¶39). *(Drafted.)*
He has the idea of reusing the thread that sewed the strips of the balloon (II.8 ¶2). *(Drafted.)*
He makes the pulleys on the lathe, on Pencroff's advice (II.12 ¶12). *(Drafted.)*
He gives the order that places the colonists in a line on the narrow bank between the river and the granite wall (II.12 ¶40). *(Drafted.)*
He decides to put the unknown to the test by moving him before the ocean and the forest edge, and does not believe he will flee (II.15 ¶70, ¶74). *(Drafted.)*
He reasons that a man sure of deliverance at a set time would have waited and not thrown the document into the sea (II.16 ¶51). *(Drafted.)*

He decides on a windmill on the heights of Grande-Vue rather than a mill at the Mercy's second fall, draws the plans, and gives the carpenters the templates to follow (II.16 ¶82, ¶85, ¶86). *(Drafted.)*
He makes soda at the Chimneys, with the reporter, the soap supply being used up (II.16 ¶99). *(Drafted.)*
He holds that Ayrton told the truth, since it was cruel enough for him (II.18 ¶14). *(Drafted.)*

He resolves to put the corral in instant communication with Granite-house, and reckons on having every element for a battery, the hardest part being the drawing of the iron wire (II.18 ¶28, ¶33). *(Drafted.)*
He tells Pencroff that counting the wheat's four hundred thousand million grains at three hundred a minute would take about five thousand five hundred years (II.18 ¶52). *(Drafted.)*
He asks the reporter, a twentieth time, whether the fire might not have been a partial eruption of the volcano or some meteor (II.20 ¶34, ¶35). *(Drafted.)*
At the sight of the ship he fears rather than hopes for her coming (III.1 ¶55). *(Drafted.)*
After the brig's sinking he says "cette fois, nous saurons !", but not what, "Plus tard ! plus tard !" (III.4 ¶4, ¶6). *(Drafted.)*
He observes the wrecked hull "dans un étonnement silencieux" (III.4 ¶60). *(Drafted.)*
At the sight of the devastated plateau he is paler than usual and holds down, with difficulty, an inner anger, saying not a word (III.10 ¶31). *(Drafted.)*
He holds that fires round a camp would suffice against jaguars and beasts, but would draw the convicts rather than stop them, so that darkness is better (III.11 ¶48). *(Drafted.)*

He proposes a bigger ship than the Bonadventure, of two hundred and fifty to three hundred tons, able to carry them to the Polynesian archipelagos or New Zealand; he finds the Scottish yacht's arrival at Tabor "fort problématique" (III.14 ¶8, ¶10). *(Drafted.)*
He draws the plan of the new vessel and fixes her gauge (III.14 ¶15). *(Drafted.)*

He conceives the plan of fortifying the corral: raising the palisaded enclosure and flanking it with a sort of blockhouse; Granite-house being inexpugnable by its position, the corral would always be the pirates' objective (III.14 ¶24). *(Drafted.)*

He sets out for his companions the pros and cons of an eruption, without exaggerating; Granite-house seems not menaced barring an earthquake, but the corral would have everything to fear if a new crater opened in the south walls of Mont Franklin (III.15 ¶5, ¶6). *(Drafted.)*
He understands that the despatch did not start from the corral but from the mysterious retreat, which an additional wire joins directly to Granite-house (III.15 ¶71). *(Drafted.)*
He greets the man on the divan by his name: "Capitaine Nemo, vous nous avez demandés ? Nous voici." (III.15 ¶147). *(Drafted.)*
He promises Nemo to carry out his last wishes, and by that promise binds his companions and himself (III.17 ¶20, ¶21, ¶37). *(Drafted.)*

He tells his friends it is useless to discuss submarine vessels: the Nautilus is not theirs, they have no right to dispose of it, and Nemo's wish that she be engulfed with him is formal, "et nous l’accomplirons" (III.17 ¶50). *(Drafted.)*

He weighs the coming eruption more gravely than Pencroff: the old lava road is still open and the crater has so far poured north, but an island of basalt on one side, granite on the other, lava to the north and loose soil to the south could be broken up by an earthquake (III.18 ¶24, ¶27). *(Drafted.)*
He tells his companions that Lincoln Island is doomed to a destruction whose cause is in itself and that nothing can avert (III.19 ¶2, ¶3). *(Drafted.)*
On the bare rock after the island's end he is calm (III.20 ¶8). *(Drafted.)*
He prays that God receive the soul of Captain Nemo, whom he calls "notre sauveur" (III.20 ¶41). *(Drafted.)*
He tells Robert Grant that where he left a culprit he finds a man "que l’expiation a refait honnête", whose hand he is proud to give (III.20 ¶48). *(Drafted.)*
He has no memory from the moment he sank until he found himself in his friends' arms (I.8 ¶67). *(Drafted.)*
He says he saw, while being carried, a mountain in the west that dominates the country (I.9 ¶60). *(Drafted.)*
He breaks Top's collar in two and calls the halves two knives (I.13 ¶26). *(Drafted.)*
He makes the bricks by hand, without moulds (I.13 ¶32). *(Drafted.)*
He guides Nab and Pencroff in carrying limestone, which gives quicklime and, with sand, mortar (I.13 ¶44). *(Drafted.)*
He has a little lime and quartz added to the clay for the pottery (I.13 ¶47). *(Drafted.)*
He will turn the colonists into smiths whenever he sees fit (I.13 ¶50). *(Drafted.)*
He tells Pencroff it is not tobacco but Chinese mugwort, tinder for them (I.13 ¶55). *(Drafted.)*
He later soaks it in potassium nitrate, of which the island has several beds (I.13 ¶56). *(Drafted.)*

He is inclined to think the beings who landed have been there only a very short time, or have only passed, since from Mount Franklin the colonists would have seen or been seen; he thinks castaways were thrown on the coast "depuis quelques semaines seulement" (II.1 ¶15). *(Drafted.)*

Harbert says that Cyrus Smith has always seemed rather to dread than to desire the presence of human beings on the island, and the reporter replies that he sees only Malays frequenting these seas (II.1 ¶44, ¶45). *(Drafted.)*
He hears Harbert's report of the view from the kauri, shakes his head and says nothing (II.1 ¶59). *(Drafted.)*
He and his companions keep Easter Sunday, 1 April, by rest and prayer (II.9 ¶68). *(Drafted.)*
He plans the next day's calculation (the plateau's height) while making tonight's sighting (I.13 ¶71). *(Drafted.)*
He watches the unknown at every moment, and his eyes do not leave the man's (II.15 ¶68, ¶88). *(Drafted.)*
He and Nab skin the two seals adroitly (I.15 ¶28). *(Drafted.)*
He says the colonists outdo "les Robinsons d’autrefois" by a hundred cubits, since they know what to do (I.19 ¶23). *(Drafted.)*
He answers Harbert's plan to store the herbs for sickness with a serious question: why be ill, "puisqu’il n’y a pas de médecins dans l’île ?" (I.19 ¶33). *(Drafted.)*
Told that four hundred thousand million grains make three million bushels, he says he knows only that he is "une bête" (I.20 ¶53). *(Drafted.)*
He would not throw to the wind a tobacco seed that multiplies three hundred and sixty thousand times (I.20 ¶61). *(Drafted.)*
He and Nab are proud of the heavy furniture made in the days of the storm, which they would not swap for Boule pieces (I.22 ¶27). *(Drafted.)*
He and Harbert had cut the purple osiers before the rains, and the colonists turn basket-makers (I.22 ¶28). *(Drafted.)*
At the mention of the lead shot he swears "Mille diables, non !", thinking of his missing molar (II.5 ¶52). *(Drafted.)*
He "already has homesickness for Granite-house" (II.5 ¶61). *(Drafted.)*
He jokes of an island where shirts grow on trees (II.5 ¶86). *(Drafted.)*
He keeps the ape's legs shackled until the plateau is closed, rightly wishing to wait (II.7 ¶30). *(Drafted.)*
He has made Jup a cane (II.8 ¶28). *(Drafted.)*
He says that were Jup as wicked as he is good, there would be no managing him (II.8 ¶29). *(Drafted.)*

His first thought in the hail, whose stones are the size of pigeon's eggs, is that his wheat field runs the most serious dangers; he runs to it and protects the crop with a big canvas, is pelted in its place, and does not complain (II.9 ¶3, ¶4). *(Drafted.)*

He holds that after the necessities one should think of comfort, which for loads and goods is indispensable, and asks the engineer for the lift he had spoken of: not so convenient to climb a long ladder when heavily loaded (II.9 ¶20, ¶24). *(Drafted.)*
He makes the glassmaker's cane, five to six feet long, by rolling a long, thin strip of iron like a gun barrel (II.9 ¶35). *(Drafted.)*
He asks to be allowed to blow glass in his turn, and blows so hard that his products take the most cheerful shapes, which he admires (II.9 ¶42). *(Drafted.)*
He measures the five bushels of the second harvest scrupulously, wants to sow all of it but for a small reserve, and expects bread and a mill (II.10 ¶10, ¶12, ¶14, ¶16). *(Drafted.)*

He is given a filled pipe by Spilett and a live coal by Harbert on 31 May, and cries 'Du tabac ! Du vrai tabac !' and 'Il ne manque donc plus rien à notre île !'; he smokes on and on, and tells his friends he will pay them back, 'à la vie, à la mort' (II.10 ¶82, ¶90, ¶91, ¶93, ¶95, ¶96, ¶101). *(Drafted.)*

He means to be away only a few days, to go and come back and see what the islet is; he asks to take only Harbert with him; he reckons that when the engineer has seen the boat well rigged and handled at sea he will no longer hesitate to let him go, and says it will be a masterpiece (II.11 ¶14, ¶22, ¶24). *(Drafted.)*
He expects no great result from the albatross as a means of correspondence (II.11 ¶38). *(Drafted.)*
He gives Jup his pipe as a present (II.12 ¶70). *(Drafted.)*
He proposes lining the hull inside with a watertight ceiling, to secure the boat's solidity (II.12 ¶80). *(Drafted.)*
He picks a young straight fir without knots for the mast, which he need only square at the foot and round at the head (II.12 ¶84). *(Drafted.)*
He counts Jup among the colony: 'Sur six ! Vous oubliez Jup.' (II.12 ¶117). *(Drafted.)*
He sees only luck in the bottle: "Cela me semble heureux, voilà tout", and "pourquoi pas ici aussi bien qu’ailleurs ?" (II.13 ¶10). *(Drafted.)*

He is satisfied with his crew and talks of rewarding them with "un quart de vin par bordée"; he laughs at his own joke when he says the sea is not so deserted, since they are on it, and asks whether they take the boat for a wreck and themselves for porpoises (II.13 ¶28, ¶37, ¶38). *(Drafted.)*
He trusts Harbert as himself at the helm and gives him the course like a commander to a helmsman (II.13 ¶31). *(Drafted.)*

He is sure the castaway is still on Tabor: he would have taken with him the arms and tools, which castaways prize as the last relics of the wreck, and had he made a boat he would have left them still less (II.14 ¶14). *(Drafted.)*
He thinks the unknown did not reach Tabor by shipwreck but was left there after some crime (II.16 ¶45). *(Drafted.)*

Smith tells him he bears three-quarters of all the colonists' tasks; Pencroff teases him that with Smith everything becomes too easy, a port with a lighthouse, a mole and a dry dock (II.15 ¶58, ¶59). *(Drafted.)*
He argues that if the castaway wrote the document seven or eight years ago and threw it in the sea, the paper could not have escaped damage by damp (II.18 ¶8). *(Drafted.)*
He once thought of counting the grains of the wheat harvest and gave it up when told how long it would take (II.18 ¶52). *(Drafted.)*
He and Nab spend much of their time on the care of the pigs (II.18 ¶54). *(Drafted.)*
He is delighted to see his portrait hang on the walls of Granite-house and stops before the display as before the richest windows of Broadway (II.18 ¶64). *(Drafted.)*

He saw the fire of 19 to 20 October, without which the Bonadventure would have passed to leeward of the island; he is sure of having seen it, with a sky of heavy clouds in which a star would not have been so low on the horizon (II.19 ¶83; II.20 ¶57, ¶61). *(Drafted.)*
He is calm only with an effort when he embraces Harbert, "son enfant" (III.3 ¶11). *(Drafted.)*

He holds, against all, that the Speedy was blown up and did not strike: there is no rock in the channel, a bed of fine sand he has often crossed at low tide, and the sea was high, so the brig had water enough; "Il tenait pour « une explosion »" (III.4 ¶44, ¶53, ¶63). *(Drafted.)*
The narrator calls him "l’entêté marin" in this dispute (III.4 ¶63). *(Drafted.)*
He and Ayrton dive to the channel bed and bring up the brig's anchors, chains and four cannon (III.4 ¶75). *(Drafted.)*
He has taken it on himself to clean the four guns, and spends hours rubbing, greasing and polishing them and their breech-gear (III.5 ¶33). *(Drafted.)*
Beside the wounded Harbert he sobs and weeps, wants to break his head against the wall, and is like a sister of mercy, like a mother at her child's bed (III.7 ¶11, ¶46). *(Drafted.)*
He says he has seen worse than a ball through the chest: "J’en ai vu bien d’autres" (III.8 ¶16). *(Drafted.)*
Spilett and Smith keep the diagnosis from him: had he heard it he would have gone mad; during the second fit he has to be taken away (III.10 ¶51, ¶53). *(Drafted.)*

When the third fit does not come he hugs the reporter to suffocation, and from then on calls him only "le docteur Spilett"; the narrator likens him to a man drawn from the bottom of an abyss (III.11 ¶12). *(Drafted.)*
He has loaded his gun with the ball that went through Harbert's chest (III.11 ¶62). *(Drafted.)*

At the corral edge he is impatient to scout at once and unwilling to obey Smith, and he vents his anger on the convicts in the roughest oaths of the seaman's repertory (III.12 ¶19, ¶21, ¶23). *(Drafted.)*
He is dismayed at the loss of the Bonadventure, of which he was so proud (III.13 ¶63). *(Drafted.)*

He says the genius might himself supply the means of getting home; he and Nab would not have shown surprise had they been told a ship of three hundred tons awaited them in Shark Gulf or Port-Ballon (III.14 ¶4, ¶5). *(Drafted.)*

He and Ayrton are the two most zealous builders of the new vessel, men not to mind the wind or the rain that soaks them to the bone; with Ayrton he pulls the pegs and copper nails from the brig's mutilated planks and ribs (III.14 ¶29; III.15 ¶9). *(Drafted.)*
He frowns that his hemisphere should be so ill-shared ("Ce n’est pas juste, cela !"), and is slow to resign himself (III.14 ¶38, ¶40). *(Drafted.)*
He and Spilett show themselves distinguished washers of linen (III.14 ¶48). *(Drafted.)*
He means to keep the name Bonadventure for the new ship, which he wants afloat in Port-Ballon within two months (III.18 ¶30). *(Drafted.)*
At the news that the island must perish he cannot hold back a big tear, and does not try to hide it (III.19 ¶22). *(Drafted.)*
The ruin of his domain plunges him into a sombre taciturnity; with hope back, he thinks only of the ship, on which all his hopes are fixed (III.19 ¶70). *(Drafted.)*
He and Ayrton make the preparations for the launch (III.19 ¶80). *(Drafted.)*
On the bare rock he is in the grip of a dull anger, and paces to and fro (III.20 ¶8). *(Drafted.)*
He proposes to proceed by method: shelter, fire and food (I.4 ¶5). *(Drafted.)*
He makes two cudgels from two stout branches broken from the first tree of the forest; Harbert wears the points on a rock (I.6 ¶18). *(Drafted.)*
With Nab, skilfully directed, he makes steel axe-heads, heated red and plunged into cold water, which take an excellent temper (I.15 ¶50). *(Drafted.)*
He recognises the jacamar as the bird that escaped the first excursion, and his shot goes off "malgré lui" (II.3 ¶24, ¶26). *(Drafted.)*
He catches crayfish by hand from the creek bank, some dozens in five minutes (II.4 ¶24, ¶27). *(Drafted.)*
He sets out by order: shelter, fire, food (I.4 ¶5). *(Drafted.)*
He blazes his way through the forest with broken branches (I.9 ¶88). *(Drafted.)*
He tries to bring down wild ducks with arrows, without result: they hardly settle and must be hit in flight (I.14 ¶38). *(Drafted.)*
He smokes with delight now that he has tobacco (II.10 ¶96). *(Drafted.)*
He suggests that the lake's water may run out through its bed and reach the sea by an underground conduit (I.16 ¶51). *(Drafted.)*
He finds a bed of saltpetre in the north of the island, at the foot of Mont Franklin (I.17 ¶48). *(Drafted.)*
He attaches little importance to the grain and is about to throw it away; Cyrus Smith tells him he has made a discovery "d’une importance extrême pour nous" (I.20 ¶43, ¶60). *(Drafted.)*
He recalls the Atlantis when the engineer speaks of a vanished continent (I.21 ¶27). *(Drafted.)*

As "le jeune naturaliste" he notes lardizabaleae and ebenaceae on the Mercy's banks, and finds wild spinach, cress, radish, turnips and other crucifers that could be "civilised" by transplanting (II.3 ¶12, ¶13). *(Drafted.)*
He climbs a tall pine with Nab and the sailor to free the balloon, and they have to show prodigies of skill (II.5 ¶88). *(Drafted.)*
He has the idea of tying a cord to an arrow, and aims "avec un soin extrême" at the ladder's dangling end (II.6 ¶32, ¶33). *(Drafted.)*
He jokes that Jup is "pas encore un maçon, mais déjà un singe", alluding to the masons' name for their apprentices (II.7 ¶43). *(Drafted.)*
He takes a pair of round-tailed gallinaceans, magnificent "alectors", that soon tame (II.7 ¶45). *(Drafted.)*

Hunting with the engineer, he keeps asking him a thousand questions and talks chemistry and physics, so that kangaroos, capybaras and agoutis pass within range and escape his gun (II.9 ¶44). *(Drafted.)*
He is the one who recognised the barking foxes of the Red Creek's sources, on his first visit there, and names them culpeux (II.12 ¶34, ¶35). *(Drafted.)*
He shoots the albatross with a gunshot that wounds its foot lightly, and would gladly keep it and tame it, but yields to Spilett's argument (II.11 ¶32, ¶33). *(Drafted.)*
He observes that nothing proves the bottle has long been afloat (II.13 ¶12). *(Drafted.)*
He judges Tabor a much smaller islet than Lincoln Island and probably, like it, the work of some submarine upheaval (II.13 ¶45). *(Drafted.)*
He remarks that the document speaks of one castaway only (II.13 ¶76). *(Drafted.)*
Thrown down by the savage, he is the first to see that it is not an ape (II.14 ¶48, ¶53). *(Drafted.)*
He hopes that with care a glimmer of intelligence can be woken in the savage, and notes how deeply his eyes lie under the brow (II.14 ¶65, ¶89). *(Drafted.)*
He hunts with the reporter, who does not let him roam the forest alone (II.17 ¶3). *(Drafted.)*
He saw the fire of 19 to 20 October, which shone like a star of the first magnitude and was certainly on the heights of Granite-house (II.20 ¶59, ¶63). *(Drafted.)*
With Spilett, aided by Jup and Top, he hunts the marshes of the tadornes (II.20 ¶77). *(Drafted.)*
He is the first to think the sail might be the Duncan, and answers Smith's fear of pirates with "Nous la défendrions !" (III.1 ¶14, ¶25). *(Drafted.)*
At the sight of the ship, while Spilett and Pencroff are nervous, he feels rather curiosity (III.1 ¶55). *(Drafted.)*
He notices that the Speedy's explosion made little noise and few wreckage, so that "le navire a plutôt coulé que sauté" (III.4 ¶30). *(Drafted.)*
He lays and fires the second gun at the rocks of the pointe de l’Épave, and is proud of his first shot (III.5 ¶37, ¶38). *(Drafted.)*
He would thank the one who saved the engineer first and then the colonists (III.5 ¶13). *(Drafted.)*
He pleads for Ayrton, who has become an honest man again, and holds that the six convicts, being six against six, have not struck for reasons of their interest (III.5 ¶58, ¶63). *(Drafted.)*
He had gathered medicinal plants on the banks of Lake Grant (III.7 ¶45). *(Drafted.)*
He understands that his wound keeps the party divided at the corral, and it is his chief trouble (III.9 ¶3). *(Drafted.)*

He is more impatient than any to be back at Granite-house, knowing how much the colonists' presence is needed there; he believes his strength will return sooner in his room, with the air and the sight of the sea (III.9 ¶45). *(Drafted.)*
In the cart he calls on all his energy, holding back by an act of will his strength ready to fail (III.9 ¶79). *(Drafted.)*
He offers Jup a place in his cart on the 15 February departure, and Jup accepts without ceremony (III.11 ¶39). *(Drafted.)*
He says they will not return to Granite-house until they have found their benefactor (III.13 ¶42). *(Drafted.)*
He takes Pencroff's hand and says they will make another Bonadventure, a bigger one, with all the ironwork and rigging of the brig at their disposal (III.13 ¶59). *(Drafted.)*
He and Gédéon Spilett, Top ahead, run oftener than any of their companions on the corral road, hunting with the excellent arms they have (III.14 ¶20). *(Drafted.)*
He answers Pencroff that he will never abandon Lincoln Island, above all if Pencroff stays, laughing and blushing at once when Pencroff speaks of his wife and children (III.15 ¶15, ¶17). *(Drafted.)*
He goes up at dawn to Grande-Vue to saddle one of the onaggas, and is the first to see the plume on the volcano (III.18 ¶12). *(Drafted.)*
He would have gone with Smith to the corral but will not vex Pencroff by being away from the yard (III.18 ¶60). *(Drafted.)*
On the bare rock he never leaves the engineer, and looks at him as if to ask a help that Smith cannot bring (III.20 ¶8). *(Drafted.)*
Weak with hunger, he and Nab begin to show signs of delirium (III.20 ¶11). *(Drafted.)*
Pencroff would leave only with Harbert (I.2 ¶35). *(Drafted.)*
He deftly draws the single match from the waistcoat lining without breaking it (I.5 ¶68). *(Drafted.)*
He draws near to Nemo, kneels, takes his hand and kisses it (III.16 ¶84). *(Drafted.)*
He sets out to hunt confident (I.9 ¶80). *(Drafted.)*
He does not complain of the meagre meal (I.9 ¶99). *(Drafted.)*
He takes his turn at the helm of the boat, relieving Pencroff every two hours through the night (II.13 ¶31). *(Drafted.)*
He draws the island's outline on Cyrus Smith's advice, and the map is made at once, with sufficient precision (I.11 ¶21). *(Drafted.)*
He would rather have names borrowed from their own country, to remind them of America (I.11 ¶62). *(Drafted.)*
He is set on stocking the larder with at least half a dozen rabbits before he quits the warren, meaning to domesticate those taken later (I.19 ¶40). *(Drafted.)*
He recalls that the island lies on the thirty-fifth parallel, which answers to Spain's in the other hemisphere, and so thinks its winters will not be hard (I.20 ¶6). *(Drafted.)*
He finds it singular that so small an island should have so varied a soil, which belongs logically only to continents of some extent (I.21 ¶23). *(Drafted.)*
He counsels prudence on learning that a gun has been fired on the island (II.1 ¶16). *(Drafted.)*
He judges it more than probable that the strangers have left the island, calling them "des naufragés provisoires" if a gale threw them ashore without wrecking their boat (II.1 ¶41, ¶43). *(Drafted.)*
He jokes about the monkeys, asking whether they take the men for degenerate brothers (II.4 ¶7). *(Drafted.)*
He wants the creek named so as not to leave their geography incomplete (II.4 ¶14). *(Drafted.)*
He reasons that the sea may have carried off all wreckage, so that finding no trace does not prove no ship was cast ashore (II.4 ¶40). *(Drafted.)*
He takes the failure to find a wreck as a consolation: no one will come to dispute Lincoln Island with them (II.5 ¶50). *(Drafted.)*
At the sight of the drifting canoe he says low to the engineer, "voilà ce que l'on peut appeler une circonstance…" (II.5 ¶114). *(Drafted.)*
He is the one who reasons that "rien n'est plus naturel": someone came in their absence and took the dwelling, "le chasseur au grain de plomb" (II.6 ¶6, ¶8). *(Drafted.)*
He says of Jup that his conversation is a little monotonous (II.6 ¶114). *(Drafted.)*
He and Harbert unpick the balloon's long seams with admirable patience (II.8 ¶2). *(Drafted.)*
He means to purge his domain of the wild beasts that take refuge in the woods of the Serpentine peninsula (II.8 ¶42). *(Drafted.)*
With Harbert he is the engineer's natural helper at the glassworks, which they do not leave for some days (II.9 ¶33). *(Drafted.)*

He raises the check of the island's position with the better sextant, reasoning that imperfect instruments may have spoiled the exactness of the observations and that verification is easy; he wonders whether the colonists are not much nearer an inhabited land than they think (II.9 ¶70, ¶72, ¶74, ¶76). *(Drafted.)*
He takes up Harbert's plan of keeping the find from Pencroff, and the plant is smuggled into Granite-house 'en fraude' (II.10 ¶29, ¶31, ¶32). *(Drafted.)*
He is curious to see Pencroff handle a harpoon; he is surprised to see a whale at so high a latitude (II.10 ¶37, ¶39). *(Drafted.)*

He has thought several times of throwing into the sea a notice in a bottle, or of trusting it to pigeons, but the distance of twelve hundred miles to any land makes that, says the narrator, pure folly; he persuades Harbert to let the albatross carry a notice (II.11 ¶31, ¶33). *(Drafted.)*
He is a little of a doctor: he judges Jup out of danger, and lets him eat as he pleases in his convalescence (II.12 ¶60, ¶62). *(Drafted.)*
He wonders whether he entrusted his last chronicle for the Herald to one of the great sea birds (II.13 ¶33). *(Drafted.)*
He proposes climbing the cone to get a summary view of the islet and so ease the search (II.13 ¶53). *(Drafted.)*
He suggests the document may have been written by a companion of the castaway, since dead (II.15 ¶27). *(Drafted.)*
He has the idea that the sight of fire may work on the savage (II.14 ¶77). *(Drafted.)*
He thinks the unknown has too grave things to say if he is silent, and that he has come back into humanity only by way of remorse (II.16 ¶9, ¶23). *(Drafted.)*
He leaves the engineer only to hunt with Harbert, for it would not be prudent to let the boy roam the forest alone (II.17 ¶3). *(Drafted.)*
He remembers that the newspapers reported Lord Glenarvan's attempt and its result, and holds Ayrton's tale true in every point (II.18 ¶13). *(Drafted.)*
He resolves to press Smith to put their companions in the way of these strange facts (II.20 ¶4). *(Drafted.)*
He and Harbert, helped by Jup and Top, hunt the vast marshes of the tadornes in the great cold and lose no shot among the ducks, snipe, teal, pintails and lapwings (II.20 ¶77). *(Drafted.)*
He reasons that an island absent from the newest charts is a reason for a ship to visit it rather than flee it (III.1 ¶27). *(Drafted.)*

He holds that the bleeding must be stopped but the wounds neither closed nor brought to scar at once, because the ball pierced within and the matter must not gather in the chest (III.7 ¶40). *(Drafted.)*

He and Pencroff show themselves distinguished washers of linen while he waits for the postman to bring his newspaper (III.14 ¶48). *(Drafted.)*

He believes the handling of a submarine like the Nautilus must be very easy and quickly learned: no storms, no collisions, and a few feet down the sea is as calm as a lake (III.17 ¶48). *(Drafted.)*
On the bare rock he is more nervous than Smith (III.20 ¶8). *(Drafted.)*
He notes the day's incidents while the others make camp (I.10 ¶48). *(Drafted.)*

He and Pencroff skin the two seals adroitly; the narrator calls him "le nègre" (I.15 ¶28). *(Drafted.)*

He is "très-désappointé de ne pouvoir rentrer dans sa cuisine" (II.6 ¶13). *(Drafted.)*

He counts Top as a colonist: 'Sur sept ! Top en vaut bien un autre !' (II.12 ¶118). *(Drafted.)*

With Spilett he does not miss his shot on the boat at the Mercy's mouth (III.3 ¶36). *(Drafted.)*

Pencroff counts on him to lend a hand in building the new ship; he and Pencroff are its two most zealous builders and work as long as they can; they pull the pegs and a great quantity of copper nails from the brig's mutilated planks and ribs (III.14 ¶13, ¶29; III.15 ¶9). *(Drafted.)*

He stands respectfully aside in a corner of the magnificent salon (III.16 ¶8). *(Drafted.)*

Aboard he refuses the cooked meat offered him, but throws himself on a raw duck with bestial greed (II.14 ¶82). *(Drafted.)*
He stays calm, silent, deaf and dumb in the forecabin, and does not stir through the night though unbound, like a wild beast that the first hours of confinement crush (II.14 ¶81, ¶92). *(Drafted.)*
He is lodged in a room of Granite-house from which he cannot escape and lets himself be led there without trouble (II.15 ¶37). *(Drafted.)*
After his flight of 10 November he is not seen again for weeks; Spilett and Harbert search the woods near Granite-house in vain (II.16 ¶95). *(Drafted.)*
He flushes the shy animals under the trees with spirit, and is recalled at once by his master (I.10 ¶21). *(Drafted.)*
He answers a light whistle from his master and comes back (I.12 ¶30). *(Drafted.)*
He fell on a litter of maras, killed three and devoured one on the spot (I.12 ¶62). *(Drafted.)*
He goes ahead of the hunters when they land to beat the banks of the Mercy (II.3 ¶13). *(Drafted.)*
His furious barking is "comme un appel désespéré" (II.6 ¶69). *(Drafted.)*

He and Jup stand guard at the foot of Granite-house at night and would soon signal the convicts (III.4 ¶74). *(Drafted.)*

He goes ahead of the party on the road, now running on the road, now making a turn in the wood, always mute; the narrator counts on him to bark at the least sign of danger, and he gives low growls as the corral nears (III.6 ¶74, ¶88). *(Drafted.)*
He barks fiercely as the engineer lifts the corral gate's latch, an instant before the shot (III.6 ¶92). *(Drafted.)*
He greets Jup, arriving over the palisade, as a friend, and barks for joy and not for anger (III.9 ¶50, ¶57). *(Drafted.)*
With Jup he is sent into the thickets before the cart passes, and when the two come back with nothing signalled there is nothing to fear from convicts or beasts (III.11 ¶46). *(Drafted.)*
He goes ahead of Harbert and Gédéon Spilett on their hunts along the corral road (III.14 ¶20). *(Drafted.)*

Beside the lake, after being very calm, he grows agitated: he paces the bank, stops short and watches the water with a paw raised, as if pointing at invisible game, barks furiously, then falls silent (I.16 ¶35). *(Drafted.)*

Called back, he returns to the bank but cannot rest; his instinct seems to lead him after some invisible being gliding under the water along the shore (I.16 ¶44). *(Drafted.)*
He plunges into the lake a second time, barking with rage, before his master can hold him (I.16 ¶53). *(Drafted.)*
He is not in the first cavern when his companions look for him (I.18 ¶31). *(Drafted.)*
His barking, heard far below, has "une rage étrange" in its broken voice (I.18 ¶40). *(Drafted.)*
In the empty great cavern he goes on barking; neither caresses nor threats silence him (I.18 ¶42). *(Drafted.)*
Urged on by his master he runs to the far end of the cavern, where his barking redoubles at the mouth of the well (I.18 ¶46). *(Drafted.)*
On the climb back he closes the march, still making singular growls (I.18 ¶81). *(Drafted.)*
Silenced by Pencroff, he stays in the room and goes on giving low growls all evening (II.11 ¶72). *(Drafted.)*
He licks Jup's hand, which hangs out of the bed, ruefully, and walks 'on tiptoe' to visit his friend (II.12 ¶57). *(Drafted.)*
He answers Pencroff's questions with small grunts that betray no ill humour; Pencroff offers him no wages to begin with, to be doubled later if he gives satisfaction (II.6 ¶109, ¶115). *(Drafted.)*
He grows used to the place easily, and looks at his new masters with an extremely curious eye (II.7 ¶30). *(Drafted.)*

In the dark he brandishes a knotty club like a mace; the narrator supposes he sees through the darkness, and he gives a shrill whistle that marks extreme jubilation with him (II.12 ¶41, ¶46). *(Drafted.)*
Nab has him nursed 'tout comme à une personne naturelle'; Top, walking on tiptoe, visits his friend and seems to approve the care, and licks his hand ruefully (II.12 ¶56, ¶57). *(Drafted.)*
Cyrus Smith cites several examples of tamed apes to whom the use of tobacco has become familiar (II.12 ¶72). *(Drafted.)*
Pencroff counts him among the colony: 'Sur six ! Vous oubliez Jup.' (II.12 ¶117). *(Drafted.)*

Smith at once judges it their dwelling (I.18 ¶51). *(Drafted.)*

It has a great hall, where on 29 October the objects of the chest are set out in order (II.2 ¶76). *(Drafted.)*
Smith offers Ayrton to spend the bad season there, where he would be better lodged than at the corral (II.20 ¶73). *(Drafted.)*
At sunset on 17 October the sun is gone "en arrière de Granite-house", the horizon to the east darkening (III.1 ¶92). *(Drafted.)*

Its fittings might escape the pirates’ eyes, Smith hopes (III.2 ¶2). *(Drafted.)*

Pencroff, delighted, sends a telegram to the corral every morning and every evening, and it never goes without an answer (II.18 ¶50). *(Drafted.)*
On 11 November the posts are in good order and the insulators intact up to pole no. 74 (III.6 ¶75). *(Drafted.)*
